                                     PROJECT NO. 58000


 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                               §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                           §                  OF TEXAS
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                      §
 THE ERCOT REGION                                   §

               TEXAS PUBLIC POWER ASSOCIATION’S RESPONSE TO
                        PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION


       The Texas Public Power Association (TPPA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the
proposal for publication (PFP) issued by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)
relating to updating wholesale and investor-owned utility (IOU) retail transmission cost recovery
in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region. These comments are submitted on
behalf of TPPA and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of any individual TPPA member.

       Formed in 1978, TPPA is the statewide association for the 72 municipally owned utilities
(MOUs) in Texas. TPPA membership also includes several electric cooperatives and joint action
agencies, as well as the Lower Colorado River Authority. TPPA members serve urban, suburban,
and rural Texas and vary in size from large, vertically-integrated utilities to relatively small
distribution-only systems. We are proud to serve approximately 5.1 million Texans across the state.
Most of our members operate within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region,
though several are located within either the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) or Midcontinent
Independent System Operator (MISO) region. MOUs offer a long track record of stability, and we
serve an essential role in providing secure and reliable power to the wholesale electricity markets
in these regions, including ERCOT. Many of our member systems have been providing stable and
reliable electric service to communities in Texas for over 100 years, and collectively, our members
provide more than 13,000 MW of generation and maintain more than 8,500 miles of high-voltage
transmission assets or more than 15% of the transmission in ERCOT.

       On July 9, 2026, the Commission issued a PFP, seeking comments by August 11, 2026.
These responses are timely filed.




TPPA Comments                                                                         Page 1 of 27
                             I.       General Comments and Recommendations

           TPPA appreciates the work the Commission and Commission Staff have devoted to this
project, including the preparation of multiple memoranda, workshops and discussions, the report,
and the study conducted by Commission Staff.

           With respect to all three proposed rules in this rulemaking project, TPPA recommends that
the Commission clarify how the rules apply to MOU TSPs that have opted into the deregulated
retail market.

           Also, TPPA notes that several sections of this rule reference proposed § 25.194, relating to
Large Load Interconnection Standards, which is still pending before the Commission. Changes to
that rule from the current proposed rule, issued in March, may impact TPPA’s comments in this
rulemaking.



                      II.        Rate Treatment to Different Large Load Customers

           Proposed § 25.192(b)(6) and proposed § 25.252(b)(3) define "large load customer" as an
entity subject to § 25.194. Under proposed § 25.194(c)(9), a large load customer is defined as an
entity requesting a new or expanded interconnection whose total expected non-coincident peak
demand at a single site equals or exceeds 75 MW. While TPPA generally supports this definition
for purposes of § 25.194, TPPA believes the rules proposed in this rulemaking, which establish a
transmission cost allocation methodology applicable across ERCOT, should apply to all loads
exceeding 75 MW, not solely those requesting a new or expanded interconnection.

           Proposed §25.194 establishes the interconnection standards for large loads seeking to
interconnect; accordingly, this rule only applies to large loads seeking a new interconnection or an
expanded interconnection. This is conversely different from Proposed § 25.192 which deals with
ongoing cost treatment for all customers interconnected to the ERCOT grid.

           Additionally, Question 4 contemplates separate rate treatment for large computational
loads. However, the Commission's report, 1 which preceded this rulemaking and served as its
foundation, concluded that changes to the transmission cost allocation methodology were

1
    Project No. 58484, Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, PUC Rules & Projects, Staff Memo and Draft
    Report (May 4, 2026).

TPPA Comments                                                                                     Page 2 of 27
 necessary because existing large load customers were avoiding TCOS charges, resulting in
residential and small commercial customers bearing a disproportionate share of those costs.
Accordingly, the data demonstrates that existing loads have historically shifted TCOS charges to
residential and small commercial customers.

       Because this rulemaking is intended to address the findings of the Commission's report, the
definition of "large load customer" should not be limited to a subset of large loads, such as large
computational loads, or only to customers requesting a new or expanded interconnection. Instead,
the rules should apply consistently to all customers with loads exceeding 75 MW.

       As discussed below, if the Commission is concerned about the impact of the revised
transmission cost allocation methodology on existing large load customers, TPPA recommends
delaying the effective date of these rules for at least 12 months following adoption. This
implementation period would allow affected customers and utilities sufficient time to prepare for
the changes and mitigate potential rate shock.

       The remainder of TPPA’s comments are written with the assumption that “large load
customer” will be defined as any entity with load exceeding 75MWs, not just those who are
seeking a new or expanded interconnection, or a subset of large loads.



                III.   Demand Charge Reduction to MOU DSP’s 12CP Load

       Proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(A) would require non-IOU DSPs to provide ERCOT with
settlement-quality meter data for each large load customer they serve. Proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(B)
would then require ERCOT to use that data to adjust each DSP's 12CP load value based on the
large load customer's demand. Specifically, ERCOT would add the difference between the
customer's large load minimum billing demand and measured 12CP load, adjusted for line losses
and annualized over the applicable period.

       TPPA notes that, although proposed § 25.192(f)(1)(B) does not directly regulate retail rate
formation, which is reserved to an MOU's governing body under PURA §§ 40.004(1) and
40.055(a)(1), the practical effect is to dictate how MOUs recover TCOS charges from large load
customers. Absent corresponding changes to MOU retail rates and tariffs, the rule could require
MOUs to recover those costs from other customer classes, resulting in residential and small

TPPA Comments                                                                         Page 3 of 27
 commercial customers in MOU service territories paying higher rates than similarly situated
customers in IOU service territories.

       As discussed in greater detail above, TPPA believes all large load customers, defined as
loads exceeding 75 MW, not just those interconnecting after the effective date of these rules or
those falling within a subset of large load customers, should be responsible for paying for their use
of the transmission system. This principle should apply equally to large load customers across
ERCOT, including in MOU service territories. However, as drafted, the rule does not recognize
the time, effort, and resources required for MOUs to revise their retail rates and tariffs through
their governing bodies to implement the Commission's policy as intended, namely ensuring that
large load customers bear TCOS charges.

       Accordingly, TPPA supports the Commission's policy objective but requests that the
effective date of the rule be delayed by at least 12 months following adoption. This additional
implementation period would provide non-IOU TSPs and DSPs, retail large load customers, and
non-IOU residential and small commercial customers sufficient time to prepare for the changes,
update retail rates and tariffs where necessary, and avoid unnecessary rate shock.



             IV.    Reduction of Transmission Interconnection Cost from TCOS

       TPPA supports efforts to reduce energy costs for residential and small commercial
customers and believes requiring large load customers, which have historically avoided paying a
proportional share of TCOS charges, to bear a greater portion of these costs is an appropriate policy
objective. The amount of transmission infrastructure that must be constructed, operated, and
maintained will not change under the proposed methodology. Rather, the proposal changes only
the mechanism by which those costs are recovered. Accordingly, the costs necessary to build,
operate, and maintain the transmission system remain fixed regardless of which customer class
ultimately pays them.

       Proposed § 25.192(e)(6) provides that transmission interconnection costs associated with
interconnection agreements executed after the effective date of the amended rule may not be
included in a TSP's transmission cost of service or transmission service rate. Similarly, proposed
§ 25.192(k) provides that a large load customer must pay the interconnecting TSP an


TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 4 of 27
 interconnection fee and provide financial security. The interconnection fee and any forfeited
financial security amounts would be used to offset a TSP’s TCOS rate, specifically the “TSP’s
transmission revenue requirement.” TPPA is concerned with this proposed approach.

       First, it is unclear to TPPA how and how frequently the Commission and TSPs will
calculate a TSP's revenue requirement and TCOS rate under the proposed rule. TPPA understands
that a TSP's revenue requirement and TCOS rate are established through comprehensive or interim
rate cases. Specifically, a TSP's Commission-approved revenue requirement and the most recent
ERCOT 4CP billing determinants are used to calculate its Commission-approved TCOS rate.
Because comprehensive or interim rate cases may occur years apart, transmission costs are
recovered annually using the revenue requirement and TCOS rate established in the most recent
comprehensive rate case. As a result, TSPs may over-recover or under-recover their transmission
costs from year to year, with those differences reconciled in the next comprehensive rate case.

       Under the proposed rule, however, interconnection costs, interconnection fees, and
forfeited financial security, all of which may vary annually, must be deducted from a TSP's revenue
requirement and reflected in its TCOS rate. TPPA understands that a comprehensive rate case must
be conducted for a utility to include other revenues as an offset to a TSP’s revenue requirement so
as to change its TCOS rate. Because comprehensive rate cases can be costly, time consuming, and
administratively burdensome, comprehensive rate cases typically occur many years apart. Because
revenue requirements and TCOS rates are not recalculated annually, it is unclear to TPPA how
these amounts will be incorporated into the annual recovery process. In addition, if the
Commission determines to adjust TSP revenue requirements and TCOS rates annually for the
offset of these other revenues, will all 46 TSPs be required to annually file a comprehensive rate
case with the Commission?

       Additionally, excluding transmission interconnection costs from a TSP's TCOS could
result in TSPs not recovering the full costs necessary to safely and reliably construct, operate, and
maintain the transmission system. As a result, there is a risk that costs that cannot be recovered
through transmission rates may instead be recovered through distribution rates, thereby continuing
to place a disproportionate burden on residential and small commercial customers and violating
the principle that distribution should not subsidize transmission.



TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 5 of 27
        Although it may appear that TSPs are fully compensated because they receive transmission
interconnection payments from large load customers, those payments do not fully account for the
costs incurred by the TSP. If a large load customer is not required to fully fund the transmission
interconnection costs prior to the TSP procuring and constructing the facilities, then the TSP must
finance the construction of transmission infrastructure, and that financing carries a cost of capital
that is not recovered through the interconnection payment itself. Accordingly, TPPA believes the
costs incurred by a TSP to build, finance, operate, and maintain its transmission facilities should
continue to be recovered through the TSP's TCOS.

       TPPA supports reducing rates for residential and small commercial customers and believes
that payments from large load customers for transmission interconnection costs can help achieve
that objective. However, TPPA recommends a different mechanism for accounting for those
payments. Specifically, TPPA recommends that transmission interconnection cost payments be
provided to DSPs as bill credits for allocation to end-use customers rather than used to reduce a
TSP's revenue requirement or TCOS rate. Depending on the methodology selected by the
Commission, reducing a TSP's transmission revenue requirement or transmission service rate by
the amount of transmission interconnection costs could result in under-recovery of the TSP's costs,
or could result in an administratively complex and costly annual rate case potentially at the expense
of residential and small commercial customers. Providing those amounts to DSPs for use as bill
credits would preserve appropriate TSP cost recovery while ensuring that end-use customers
receive the intended financial benefit.

       Ideally, bill credits would be allocated among DSPs in a manner that benefits end-use
customers across ERCOT. TPPA is eager to work with the Commission and other stakeholders to
develop an equitable methodology for distributing those credits.

       Ultimately, TPPA believes this alternative approach would accomplish the Commission's
objective of reducing costs for residential and small commercial customers and administratively
complexity and regulatory burdens while ensuring that TSPs remain financially whole and have
the resources necessary to safely and reliably construct, operate, and maintain the transmission
system.




TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 6 of 27
     V.      Transition from 4CP to 12CP Allocation, Updates to TSP’s TCOS Rates, Workshop

           Proposed § 25.192(l)2 provides transition requirements for moving from the current 4CP
methodology to the proposed new methodology.

           TPPA seeks clarification regarding the transition from the current 4CP-based TCOS
methodology to the proposed 12CP-based methodology. Specifically, will a TSP continue to use
its existing Commission-approved 4CP TCOS rate until its next comprehensive rate case, with
only the billing determinants on allocation of the costs changing from 4CP to 12CP in the interim?
If so, TPPA requests clarification regarding how this transition will ensure appropriate cost
recovery. If not, TPPA requests clarification regarding how this transition will be implemented
and how the resulting TCOS rate will be determined. TPPA also seeks clarity on when ERCOT
will file the updated 12CP billing determinants, as the 4CP billing determinants are still under
review for 2025. While TPPA believes many aspects of this process should be addressed in the
adopted rule, TPPA also believes the Commission should convene a workshop to identify all
existing and proposed process changes and ensure that TDSPs, the Commission, and ERCOT have
a common understanding of their respective roles, responsibilities, and expectations for
implementing the newly proposed processes and managing the transition to those processes.

           Additionally, TPPA continues to recommend this approach and requests that the amended
rule not become effective until at least 12 months after adoption. A 12-month transition period
would provide non-IOU DSPs sufficient time to amend and update their tariffs through their
governing bodies, as well as revise contracts and rates with existing customers that may be affected
by the changes proposed in this rulemaking. This period would also provide the Commission and
IOU DSPs sufficient time to process the new and amended tariffs necessary to implement the
proposed changes.

           This transition period would also allow the Commission sufficient time to initiate a separate
project and evaluate the appropriate treatment of wholesale storage load and export flows under
the revised transmission cost allocation methodology. Delaying implementation would reduce the
likelihood that the methodology would need to be revised multiple times and would instead allow




2
    Proposed § 25.192(l)(1), which is incorrectly labeled as subsection "(j).”

TPPA Comments                                                                              Page 7 of 27
 the Commission to implement a comprehensive methodology after determining whether wholesale
storage load and export flows should be subject to TCOS charges.



              VI.     Wholesale Transmission Service at Distribution Voltage Tariff

        Proposed § 25.192(c)(2) requires all TSPs that receive a request or have a customer
utilizing transmission service at distribution voltage to file a transmission service at distribution
voltage tariff as part of an application for Commission approval.

        This language appears to attempt to overturn, by rule, several recent orders that determined
that a TSP that provides both tariffed transmission service and tariffed transmission service at
distribution voltage does not need to simultaneously update both tariffs.3

        TPPA believes this issue was correctly decided, both by the presiding ALJs and the
Commission itself, which declined to overturn an ALJ’s decision not to certify the issue to the
Commissioners. TPPA is concerned that this rule, which purportedly focuses on needed changes
to ERCOT-wide transmission cost allocation, also includes an item that overturns longstanding
Commission precedent on an entirely separate issue. TPPA believes these changes should be
removed from the rule entirely, and if Commission Staff believes these changes are truly necessary,
they should be proposed in a distinct rulemaking focusing on that specific issue.

        Nonetheless, TPPA believes that this change, if adopted, would be in conflict with statutory
limits on the Commission’s jurisdiction. The Commission's authority to review and set rates for
municipally owned utilities (MOUs) is governed by PURA Chapter 35. Chapter 35 does not grant
the Commission authority to review or approve rates associated with distribution facilities. Instead,
PURA § 35.007(a) provides that, "except as provided by Subsection (b), an electric utility that
owns or operates transmission facilities shall file a tariff in compliance with Commission rules
adopted under Section 35.006."4 Neither PURA § 35.006 nor Subsection (b) of PURA § 35.007

TPPA Comments                                                                                      Page 8 of 27
 grants the Commission authority to review or approve tariffs related to distribution facilities.5
Further, PURA § 40.055(a)(1) states that a MOU’s governing body has the exclusive jurisdiction
to set rates for distribution, excluding only wholesale transmission rates.

           By contrast, PURA Chapter 36 grants the Commission broad jurisdiction to review and
approve rates for electric utilities, and under Chapter 36, "electric utility" does not include MOUs
or electric cooperatives. The Legislature's decision to provide comprehensive rate oversight
authority in Chapter 36, while omitting comparable authority in Chapter 35, demonstrates that the
Commission's jurisdiction over MOU rates is limited to those expressly identified in Chapter 35.
Accordingly, PURA does not authorize the Commission to review or approve rates associated with
MOU distribution facilities.



                                         VII.      Co-Located Large Loads

           Through SB6, letters from members of the Texas Legislature, and the Governor's June 10
and August 3 letters, state leadership has made clear that it supports the interconnection of large
loads in Texas while ensuring those customers are interconnected in a manner that protects
residential and small commercial customers from bearing unnecessary costs. Consistent with that
objective, the Commission was directed to review the existing TCOS allocation methodology to
ensure that residential and small commercial customers do not bear a disproportionate share of the
costs associated with serving large load customers. TPPA notes, however, that the proposed rules
do not appear to address the treatment of large load customers that are co-located with generation
resources, whether through a net metering arrangement or by developing their own generation
resource.

           TPPA believes that large load customers should continue to pay TCOS charges in both co-
location scenarios based on their gross load rather than their net imports from the transmission

TPPA Comments                                                                                               Page 9 of 27
 system. Under the proposed framework, a co-located large load generally would pay TCOS
charges only on its net imports from the grid, even though it continues to benefit from transmission
infrastructure funded by other customers that is capable of meeting its gross load.6 This result is
inconsistent with the purpose of this rulemaking.

         Under a net metering arrangement, 7 a large load chooses to co-locate with an existing
generation resource, regardless of whether that generation resource qualifies as an "existing
generation resource" under SB6. Transmission facilities have already been constructed to
interconnect that generation resource so that its output can be delivered to end-use customers
across ERCOT. As a result, when a large load elects to co-locate with an already interconnected
generation resource, the need for additional transmission facilities to serve the large load is
significantly reduced because the necessary transmission infrastructure has already been built.

         Importantly, however, those transmission facilities were not funded by either the
generation resource or the co-located large load. Rather, they were funded through TCOS charges
paid by end-use customers across ERCOT, primarily residential and small commercial customers.
Once the large load begins consuming a substantial portion of the generation resource's output
behind the point of interconnection, the transmission facilities originally constructed to export that
energy may become significantly underutilized, despite having been funded by customers across
the state.

TPPA Comments                                                                                        Page 10 of 27
            While SB6 establishes protections for net metering arrangements involving "existing
generation resources," it does not adequately address newly constructed generation resources.
Under the Commission's implementation of SB6, TSPs interconnecting newly constructed
generation resources may recover all, or a substantial portion, of their transmission interconnection
costs through TCOS rates. Those same generation resources could subsequently co-locate with a
large load under a net metering arrangement, substantially reducing the public benefit of the
transmission facilities that ratepayers funded. Unlike "existing generation resources" subject to
SB6, there are currently no statutes, Commission rules, or ERCOT Protocols requiring newly
constructed generation resources to make their generation available to the ERCOT market during
emergency conditions. As a result, customers across ERCOT could ultimately fund transmission
facilities that provide little or no ongoing system-wide benefit.

           A similar concern exists where a large load develops its own generation resource. Although
current rules generally do not contemplate this arrangement, they do not clearly prevent it. 8 A
generation resource may interconnect as a transmission-level generator under § 25.195 and the
TSP would recover the majority of its interconnection costs through TCOS rates. The large load
could locate behind that generation resource and incur only modest additional interconnection
costs because the necessary transmission facilities were already funded through TCOS. Moreover,
the definition of "transmission-level generator" requires only that the resource generate electricity
"for compensation," but neither the Commission rules nor the ERCOT Protocols clearly define
what constitutes compensation. Consequently, a generation resource could consume nearly all of
its output behind the meter while selling only a nominal amount of energy or ancillary services
into the ERCOT market, or by settling limited excess production as a settlement-only generator,
and still arguably satisfy the definition.

        Accordingly, TPPA recommends that the Commission address both co-location scenarios
in this rulemaking. Specifically, TPPA recommends that co-located large load customers
participating in net metering arrangements, regardless of whether they are paired with an existing
generation resource under SB6, as well as large load customers that develop their own generation
resources, be required to pay TCOS charges based on their gross load rather than their net load.
To accomplish this, the customers' 12CP load should be determined using the gross load meter
rather than the net meter, and the data used to calculate any minimum demand charge should
likewise be collected from the gross load meter.



                         VIII. Responses to Commission Questions

1) Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different non-
coincident (NCP) demands?
       At this time, TPPA has no comments in response to this question.



2) Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
       a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
       b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
       c. extended to a longer time period?
3) Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large load
minimum billing demand:
       a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
          some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
          demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in
          phases over the years, and how?
       b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
          load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
          customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
          year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
          weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
          over the years, and how?
       The following comments respond to Questions 2 and 3.



TPPA Comments                                                                       Page 12 of 27
        As noted in prior TPPA comments, TPPA believes the discussions surrounding SB6 made
clear the Legislature's intent to ensure that residential and small commercial customers are not
burdened with the costs associated with interconnecting large loads. Significant transmission
system upgrades are being planned to accommodate anticipated large load interconnections to the
ERCOT system, both through ERCOT's load forecast and through regional transmission projects
driven by specific large load interconnection requests. While these upgrades may provide broader
system benefits, they are primarily driven by large load demand and would not otherwise be
necessary to directly serve residential and small commercial customers. Accordingly, those
customers should not bear responsibility for the costs of these upgrades.

       TPPA therefore believes that any TCOS methodology adopted by the Commission must
ensure that residential and small commercial customers do not pay for these upgrades or, at a
minimum, that large load customers cannot avoid paying for them in a manner that shifts costs
onto other customer classes.

       At this time, TPPA does not support assigning transmission system upgrade costs directly
to individual customers through the interconnection process because doing so would be highly
complex. However, if the Commission chooses to pursue this approach, it should recognize that
assigning costs at the time of interconnection will not necessarily reflect the long-term benefits
provided by the facilities or each customer's actual use of the transmission system.

       Alternatively, TPPA recommends that the Commission adopt a TCOS methodology that
appropriately allocates transmission costs among customer classes based on their use of and benefit
from the transmission system, ensuring that no customer class bears a disproportionate share of
those costs.

       Because proposed § 25.194 contemplates assigning certain transmission system upgrade
costs directly to interconnecting large load customers, but has not yet been adopted, it is unclear
whether those customers ultimately will bear these costs directly or how such payments would
affect TCOS recovery. TPPA believes the appropriate TCOS allocation methodology depends, in
significant part, on whether interconnecting large load customers are required to directly fund the
transmission upgrades necessary to accommodate their interconnection.

       If interconnecting large load customers are required to directly pay all transmission system
upgrade costs associated with their interconnection, TPPA believes the minimum demand charge

TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 13 of 27
 should be phased out over a 20-year period. This approach recognizes that the customer has already
funded a substantial portion of the transmission infrastructure needed to serve its load while
preserving an incentive to reduce demand during system peaks through TCOS charge avoidance
behavior. Alternatively, if interconnecting large load customers are not required to directly pay
transmission system upgrade costs at the time of interconnection, TPPA recommends extending
the minimum demand charge over a 40-year period to better align with the average useful life of
many transmission facilities.

       Similarly, if a large load customer directly funds the transmission system upgrade costs
associated with its interconnection, its minimum demand charge should not be set above its cost
of service because the customer will have already paid for a substantial portion of the transmission
infrastructure necessary to serve its load. Instead, the charge should be established at a level that
reasonably reflects the costs associated with the customer's continued use of the transmission
system, including facilities constructed before the customer's interconnection, and the ongoing
operation and maintenance of the transmission network. Conversely, if interconnecting large load
customers are not required to directly fund transmission system upgrade costs, then TPPA supports
a minimum demand charge that collects significant ongoing payments over time. In that
circumstance, the demand charge should be designed to recover the costs of the transmission
upgrades constructed to accommodate the large load, while also reflecting the customer's use of
existing transmission facilities, and the ongoing costs of operating and maintaining the
transmission system.

       Regarding the application of the minimum demand charge to existing large load customers,
TPPA reiterates its recommendation that the rule apply uniformly to all large loads and not create
subsets or exemptions. Consistent with that recommendation, TPPA recommends that existing
large loads be subject to the minimum demand charge for a period equal to the difference between
the applicable phase-out period and the number of years the load has already been energized.

       TPPA also recommends that the rule clearly specify how the phase-out period will be
determined based on a large load's ramp schedule and how the phase-out period will apply to any
new incremental load installed beyond the customer's initial planned or previously connected load.

       Regardless of the demand charge ultimately adopted, TPPA supports a methodology that

agencies, as well as the Lower Colorado River Authority. TPPA members serve urban, suburban,
and rural Texas and vary in size from large, vertically-integrated utilities to relatively small
distribution-only systems. We are proud to serve approximately 5.1 million Texans across the state.
Most of our members operate within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region,
though several are located within either the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) or Midcontinent
Independent System Operator (MISO) region. MOUs offer a long track record of stability, and we
serve an essential role in providing secure and reliable power to the wholesale electricity markets
in these regions, including ERCOT. Many of our member systems have been providing stable and
reliable electric service to communities in Texas for over 100 years, and collectively, our members
provide more than 13,000 MW of generation and maintain more than 8,500 miles of high-voltage
transmission assets or more than 15% of the transmission in ERCOT.
